papers.title: Type 1 immunity linked to CMV exposure improves long-term survival in sepsis without shock
papers.abstract: Dysregulated immune responses are at the core of sepsis pathology and can drive both acute organ dysfunction and long-term morbidity and mortality. To better understand the association between specific immune histories, perturbations and sepsis outcomes, we combined immune phenotyping, functional cytokine production assays and antibody repertoire profiling. While sepsis immune profiles were highly heterogeneous, we identified a strong association between the frequency of CXCR3-expressing CD4 memory T cells at time of enrollment and six-month survival in sepsis without shock. Surprisingly, the same population was linked to improved organ function trajectories in septic shock patients but did not influence six-month survival, highlighting the importance of considering physiological states to define immune predictors. Finally, phage display profiling revealed that these Th1 cells were generally expanded in CMV-seropositive individuals, suggesting that previous and latent infections may modulate sepsis outcomes.

papers.title: Innate Immune Dysregulation Precedes Clinical Onset in Neuromyelitis Optica
papers.abstract: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is a disabling inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease characterized by pathogenic aquaporin 4 (AQP4) autoantibodies. The biological events that precede clinical onset remain unknown. In a unique longitudinal NMOSD cohort from the U.S. Department of Defense Serum Repository, with samples collected up to 24 years before onset, we applied discovery proteomics (~5,400 proteins), pan-viral antibody profiling (VirScan), and in silico analyses to characterize preclinical NMOSD versus matched healthy controls. Innate immune activation, particularly CXCL1 elevation, was the dominant immunological feature of preclinical NMOSD, preceding onset by ~12.7 years. AQP4-IgG was detectable more than 3 years before onset, while CNS injury markers increased only after disease manifestation. VirScan identified enhanced CMV-specific antibody reactivity following AQP4- IgG seroconversion, and network analyses revealed interactions between NMOSD-associated and CMV-derived proteins. Together, these findings establish a novel multi-hit model of NMOSD, with implications for understanding antibody-mediated autoimmunity more broadly.

papers.title: Pleiotropy links host axes of defense against a pathogen
papers.abstract: Organisms face ubiquitous threats from pathogens, and in response hosts have evolved a cascade of defenses to avoid, resist, or tolerate infection. While these stepwise defenses may act independently, they can be pleiotropically linked via shared molecular mechanisms, regulation, and crosstalk. Here, we tested the extent to which pleiotropy shapes multiple axes of defense using knockouts of 16 single genes involved in innate immunity of Caenorhabditis elegans against the opportunistic bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Host genotype had variable effects on components of host defense. Traits such as infection-induced mortality and body size varied frequently across host genotypes, while behavioral avoidance, bacterial uptake, and susceptibility to bacterial colonization varied less frequently. Broadly, pleiotropy between defenses was common, driving patterns of variation that linked several traits together. However, important components of defense like mortality, avoidance, and susceptibility to colonization were more independent from one another. Our results show that pleiotropy between defenses can be common, highlighting the importance of moving beyond single phenotypes to understand multiple dimensions of host-pathogen interactions.

papers.title: Alternative splicing use ratio is not conserved between human and mouse immune cells
papers.abstract: Most human genes have mouse orthologs. However, orthology at the level of exons and alternative splicing events is not well defined, and the use of alternative splicing events in immune cell types has not been compared between human and mouse. We mapped exons and alternative splicing events between human and mouse. Based on this mapping, the use ratio of orthologous alternative splicing events was compared between human and mouse immune cell types and fibroblasts. Out of the 1,823 human-mouse orthologous alternative splicing events that are expressed in the five tested immune cell types, most (62-67%) showed a significant difference in use ratio between human and mouse, and less than third (21-25%) retained the same ratio. Our results reveal both conserved and divergent alternative splicing usage ratio, and highlight the dynamic evolution of alternative splicing regulation across human and mouse immune cell types. By integrating exon orthology with observed splicing patterns, our analysis provides a functional framework for studying mammalian splicing ratio evolution beyond static transcript annotations.

papers.title: Sustained antigenic engagement programs multidimensional CTL states with distinct cytotoxic capacities
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate infected or malignant cells through repeated target-cell encounters, yet how they sustain cytotoxic activity during extended antigenic stimulation remains poorly understood. In particular, it remains unclear whether preserved population-level killing reflects maintenance of a uniform effector phenotype or diversification into functionally distinct CTL populations. Here, we combined live-cell imaging, high-dimensional cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, phenotypic trajectory analysis, population sorting, and rechallenge killing assays to define how human clonal CTLs remodel during sustained antigenic engagement. Prior antigen encounter altered the kinetics and pattern of target-cell membrane permeabilization but did not compromise overall subsequent killing upon rechallenge. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling after prolonged engagement revealed broad remodeling of antigen-experienced CTLs and heterogeneous cytotoxic transcriptional programs. Time-resolved scRNA-seq further showed that these functional dimensions remodeled with distinct kinetics, with rapid induction of activation- and cytotoxicity-associated programs, later remodeling of vesicular-trafficking programs, and progressive reduction of adhesion/ contact interaction -associated programs. High-dimensional cytometry showed that this temporal remodeling was accompanied by progressive redistribution of CTLs across a multidimensional protein-expression landscape defined by distinct combinations of cytotoxic, vesicular/degranulation, activation, cytokine, adhesion, and regulatory features. Phenotypic trajectory analysis organized this protein landscape along a temporal remodeling axis, with early lytic-granule-rich profiles giving way to multiple late-engaged phenotypes with distinct combinations of functional protein features. Surface-marker-defined late CTL populations displayed distinct killing capacities upon rechallenge, demonstrating that preserved population-level cytotoxicity can coexist with substantial functional heterogeneity. Finally, CAR T cells exposed to CD19+ targets retained cytotoxic activity upon rechallenge and acquired multidimensional phenotypic features that partially overlapped with the remodeling framework identified in clonal CTLs. Reanalysis of longitudinal patient-derived CAR T-cell transcriptomes further showed that related functional programs were dynamically organized after infusion, with the features distinguishing responder and non-responder tisa-cel samples changing between the infusion product and day 7. Together, these findings indicate that sustained CTL killing is accompanied by progressive multidimensional remodeling and diversification rather than maintenance of a fixed effector phenotype. Our findings support a model in which population-level cytotoxic activity can be maintained while the CTLs composing that population progressively diversify into functionally distinct states during sustained antigenic engagement.

papers.title: A CAR T cell-amplified suppressive B cell circuit in AML
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is constrained by a hostile bone marrow niche. Here we identify atypical memory B cells (Batyp) as a suppressive population within this microenvironment. Across single cell and flow cytometry cohorts, Batyp were expanded in AML, and their molecular and phenotypic profiles resembled those of atypical B cells associated with chronic inflammatory conditions. Batyp were polarized within the AML microenvironment, and this was amplified by CAR T cell-AML interactions. Mechanistically, polarization was dependent on Toll-like receptor, interferon and CD70-CD27 signaling. Batyp suppressed T cell and CAR T cell responses via PD-1- and TGF-beta signaling, and were enriched in non-responding patients with AML and myeloma. CD180-directed CAR T cells, targeting an antigen shared by Batyp and AML blasts, resisted suppression in vitro and cleared disease in B cell-humanized xenografts while sparing hematopoietic stem cells, with B cell engagement further enhancing their expansion. CAR T cells thus reinforce their own suppressive niche through Batyp polarization, a constraint that can be relieved by dual blast- and B cell-targeting strategies.

papers.title: IL-2 and CD40L can establish and sustain a human B cell-mediated immune regulatory network
papers.abstract: B cells can control inflammation, but the factors governing B cell-mediated immune regulatory network remain unclear. We report that IL-2/CD40L enable class-switched memory (CSM) B cells to acquire an immunosuppressive phenotype characterized by the expression of surface TIGIT as well as multiple other inhibitory receptors (PD-1, LAG-3, GITR, CD39, and CTLA-4) and soluble molecules (IL-10, granzyme B, and IL-35). TIGIT+ CSM B cells expressing functional CCR9 exhibit significant defects in total immunoglobulin secretion, while preserving IgA2 secretion. Furthermore, IL-2/CD40L-induced ex vivo-generated TIGIT+ CSM B cells suppress human T cell-mediated inflammation in a xenogeneic mouse model of acute graft-versus-host disease, while promoting IL-10-producing regulatory T cell (Treg) response. These findings identify IL-2/CD40L as key drivers of a B cell-mediated immune regulatory network, especially by generating TIGIT+ CSM B cells that can further promote Treg response. This study supports the development of TIGIT+ B cell-based therapy models for inflammatory diseases.

papers.title: CXCL9-Dependent Immune Networks of Spontaneous Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in a Murine Subcutaneous Tumor Model
papers.abstract: Recent discoveries have identified human tumor tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) as organized clusters of innate and adaptive immune cells and stromal cells. Cancer-associated TLS can promote tumor clearance and enhance responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) immunotherapy. However, the absence of TLS in conventional mouse tumor models, particularly subcutaneous transplant models, limits experimental manipulation and study of TLS development. By tuning tumor antigen expression, we have generated a subcutaneous tumor model that naturally forms TLS within the immune-hot, vasculature-rich peritumoral adipose tissue. These TLS were identified as clusters of B and T cells in close proximity to high endothelial venules. TLS organization was underpinned by spatially compartmentalized chemokine expression, with CCL21 produced in the T cell zone of perivascular TLS and CXCL13 present in the B cell region. Single cell transcriptomic sequencing showed that the immune composition in the TLS forming peritumoral tissue resembled human cancer TLS signatures. Upon anti-PD-L1 ICB treatment, TLS underwent expansion, which was associated with increased interferon responses in macrophages and coincided with tumor clearance. We further identified the interferon-inducible chemokine CXCL9 as a key regulator of the TLS microenvironment. CXCL9-expressing macrophages populated TLS, interacting with B cells following ICB treatment. CXCL9 deficiency reduced B cell recruitment to peritumoral tissue and TLS formation. Further T and B cell receptor sequencing indicated a CXCL9-dependent promotion of antigen-specific responses within the tumor and TLS niche. Combined, these findings establish a tractable subcutaneous model of naturally arising tumor TLS and define the cellular and molecular networks that regulate their formation and function. This provides a platform to dissect how TLS develop and test strategies that promote TLS formation to enhance cancer therapy.

papers.title: Beyond Better Models: Barriers and a Path Forward in Generalisable TCR Antigen Specificity Prediction
papers.abstract: T cells are at the centre of adaptive immunity, protecting the organism against infection and cancer. T cell receptors (TCRs), expressed on the surface of T cells, enable the recognition of target cells through interactions with peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) molecules. Reliable, large-scale mapping of TCRs to their cognate pMHCs remains a holy grail of modern systems immunology, with far-reaching implications for cancer immunotherapy, vaccine development, and the understanding and treatment of autoimmune diseases. While exhaustive experimental mapping remains intractable due to the enormous combinatorial sequence space of TCRs and pMHCs, computational approaches offer a promising alternative. Consequently, we have witnessed increasingly sophisticated computational models of TCR antigen specificity, from small neural networks to deep generative models and large protein language models. However, several independent benchmarks have shown that these models, despite their size and sophistication, largely fail to generalise to TCRs or pMHCs not present in the data available during model development. Here, we investigate possible reasons for this and suggest a path forward to generalisable TCR:pMHC prediction. First, our analysis of the largest public repositories of TCR:pMHC data reveals significant biases towards a small number of antigens and MHC molecules, sparse sampling of TCR sequence space per pMHC, as well as inconsistencies and inaccuracies in data collation. Second, we show the importance of carefully setting up model evaluation to measure discrimination based on antigen specificity instead of confounding factors present in the evaluation data. Finally, we highlight the need for and propose how best to match the evaluation metric with the specific downstream application of the predictions. Our investigation suggests that we, as a community, need more representative and better curated data, and a robust set of metrics and benchmarks to guide future model development towards generalisable TCR:pMHC specificity prediction.

papers.title: B cell response to HCMV gH/UL116 elicits neutralizing and FcγR-activating antibodies
papers.abstract: Humoral immune mechanisms that can contribute to limiting HCMV disease include neutralizing antibodies that block viral entry and Fc-mediated effector functions that promote elimination of infected cells. Here, we identify the gH/UL116 envelope complex as a naturally immunogenic target that elicits antibodies capable of mediating both of these immune mechanisms. Using single-cell sorting of antigen-specific memory B cells, we isolated gH/UL116-reactive monoclonal antibodies from HCMV-seropositive donors. Epitope mapping showed that gH binding was required for virus neutralization, whereas UL116 targeting was associated with potent and broad Fc{gamma} receptor (Fc{gamma}R) activation. Furthermore, cryo-electron microscopy provided high-resolution structures revealing how UL116-specific antibodies bind gH/UL116. In mice, gH/UL116 immunization elicited serum IgG responses whose binding titers strongly correlated with both neutralization and mouse Fc{gamma}R activation. Together, these findings provide an epitope-level map linking antibody specificity to neutralization and Fc{gamma}R activation across HCMV gH-associated complexes and position gH/UL116 as a promising HCMV vaccine candidate.

papers.title: Dual blockade of IL-18 and IL-4Rα by a bispecific antibody for improved treatment of atopic dermatitis
papers.abstract: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis primarily driven by type 2 immunity, with additional type 1 and type 3 components that may limit the benifit of ILRalpha blockade alone. Interleukin18 (IL18), an epithelial alarmin genetically associated with AD and correlated with disease severity, has been implicated as an upstream amplifier of this mixed inflammatory response. Objective: To assess whether concurrent IL18 neutralization and IL4Ralpha; blockade with a bispecific antibody provides broader and more balanced suppression of AD relevant type 1, type 2, and type 3 pathways than single target inhibition. Methods: We generated FJ0125, a bispecific antibody comprising human IL18 binding protein fused to a novel humanized anti IL4Ralpha antibody, and characterized its binding, signaling, and functional activity in vitro and in vivo. The activity was evaluated in human group 2 innate lymphoid cell and primed Th2 cell assays, a keratinocyte & dendritic cell & T cell coculture system, and an MC903/Staphylococcus aureus induced dermatitis model in human IL4/IL4Ralpha; knock in mice. Results: FJ0125 bound to IL18 and IL4Ralpha; with high affinity, engaged both targets, inhibited IL4/IL13 signaling with dupilumab comparable potency, and neutralized human and mouse IL18. In vitro, FJ0125 more effectively suppressed IL18 driven lymphocyte activation and type 1, type 2, and type 3 cytokine production than IL18BPFc or IL4Ralpha; monotherapy. In vivo, FJ0125 reduced multitype cytokines, improved dermatitis, lowered serum IgE, and abrogated the paradoxical IL22 increase observed with selective IL4Ralpha; blockade. Conclusion: Dual IL18/IL4Ralpha; blockade with FJ0125 achieves coordinated suppression of multitype inflammation and represents a mechanistically substantiated therapeutic strategy for AD.

papers.title: Accelerating Molecular Dynamics with Hydrogen Mass Repartitioning to Prioritize Immunogenic Neoantigens for Cancer Vaccines through Peptide HLA Binding Free Energy Calculations
papers.abstract: Personalized neoantigen based vaccines have progressed from concept to clinical evidence for some of the most aggressive human tumors, yet a key challenge remains: determining which candidates should be prioritized for vaccine inclusion. Public neoantigens, shared across tumor subtypes and patient populations, offer potential as off the shelf candidates for broad spectrum immunotherapy. Candidate selection relies on in silico pipelines that estimate binding; however, binding affinity alone is an imperfect marker of immunogenicity. Molecular dynamics (MD) combined with endpoint free energy methods estimates binding free energy directly from simulated trajectories, and hydrogen mass repartitioning (HMR) mitigates the computational cost of hydrogen involving bond vibrations. This study assessed whether HMR accelerated MD can prioritize immunogenic neoantigens through peptide HLA binding free energy calculations and quantified the trade off between accuracy and computational cost. Ten immunogenic public neoantigens (seven paired with their wild type counterparts and three frameshift neoantigens analyzed as unpaired references) were modeled in complex with their HLA I alleles, built de novo using AlphaFold3 and propagated with a 4 fs HMR time step. Mean binding free energy was computed across ten replicas per complex, and each SNV pair was scored concordant with experimental data when the neoantigen formed a more favorable complex than its wild type. Free energies were recomputed at 100 to 500 ns to identify the shortest trajectory preserving reliable ranking. Free energy calculations reproduced experimental concordance for six of seven SNV pairs and were inconclusive for TP53 R8H. Frameshift neoantigens yielded comparable values. Most complexes retained both peptide termini anchored to the HLA groove throughout, and RMSD and RMSF metrics agreed with one another and with the free energy rankings. The PIK3CA E545K (E11K) pair showed the most distinctive signature: the peptides engaged the groove almost identically over P1 to P8, with the entire difference confined to the C terminal pocket, where loss of the wild type's anchor also disrupted its backbone anchor. This pair showed the largest free energy separation in the panel, and restricting analysis to bound frames confirmed a substantial electrostatic and van der Waals advantage favoring the neoantigen. These findings support HMR accelerated binding free energy MD as a practical refinement step for neoantigen prioritization and its application to assessing public neoantigens for cancer vaccine design.

papers.title: Persistently activated virus-specific CD8 T cells indicate antigen-driven immune aberrations in long COVID
papers.abstract: Long COVID (LC) affects millions of people worldwide, yet its driving mechanisms remain incompletely defined and no treatment has been approved. Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 and reactivation of herpesviruses have been implicated in LC, but direct detection of these viral antigens in blood and tissues has been challenging. T cells are exquisitely sensitive to viral antigens, survey organs throughout the body, and can be readily sampled in peripheral blood. Using high-dimensional spectral flow cytometry and single-cell sequencing approaches with multiplexed peptide/HLA tetramers, we profiled virus-specific T cells from hundreds of people with LC and recovered controls. We identified a subset of people with LC that maintained elevated activation of CD8 T cells targeting SARS-CoV-2 spike and/or lytic antigens from Epstein-Barr virus, but not other viral specificities. Spike-specific cells in LC expressed genes linked to TCR stimulation, terminal effector differentiation, and exhaustion and demonstrated reduced functionality upon cognate peptide stimulation ex vivo. Thus, T cells from a subset of people with LC are likely chronically stimulated by persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigens. These findings establish the use of T cells as biosensors of persisting antigen in LC and other disease settings and may help develop new therapeutic strategies for LC.

papers.title: Single-cell profiling of physically interacting immune cells using image-guided sorting
papers.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics of cell-cell complexes offers key insights into in vivo immune interactions, yet distinguishing true physical contacts from artifacts remains challenging. Here, we integrated spectral imaging cell sorting with physical cell deconvolution to separate circulating T cell-monocyte doublets from tuberculosis patients into physically interacting (in-contact) and non-interacting (coincidental) populations. Single-cell sequencing of individual cell partners revealed that physical contact is associated with robust signatures distinct from singlets, including unidirectional monocyte-to-T cell RNA transfer, heightened metabolic activity and T cell cytotoxicity, and a trend toward antigen-specific enrichment. These signatures spanned all T cell and monocyte subpopulations, reflecting a global program of T cell-monocyte engagement. Coincidental doublets displayed intermediate transcriptional profiles between singlet and in-contact states, suggesting the presence of recently disrupted or forming physical pairs. This framework provides high-fidelity deconvolution of cellular interactions, uncovering signatures governing T cell-monocyte communication in human disease.

papers.title: Evolution of SARS-CoV-2 reshapes upper airway immunity in children
papers.abstract: Children were relatively protected from severe COVID-19 during the early pandemic a phenomenon linked to rapid and heightened innate immune responses in the upper-airways. Although adult upper-airway antiviral responses varied across successive SARS-CoV-2 waves, whether viral evolution similarly reshaped pediatric mucosal immunity remains unclear. Here we used single-cell transcriptomics to profile 229,533 upper-airway cells from 68 unvaccinated children including 17 uninfected controls, spanning the wild-type SARS-CoV-2, Alpha, Delta and Omicron waves. Epithelial interferon responses were primarily determined by time since symptom onset but were, unlike in adults, independent of disease severity. During early infection, anti-viral responses differed across variants without following a progressive pattern of attenuation. Alpha and Delta elicited the strongest interferon programs across epithelial and immune cell populations, whereas Omicron exhibited a shift towards macrophage cytokine signaling and T-cell cytotoxicity. These findings reveal variant-specific remodeling of pediatric upper-airway immunity that fundamentally differs from that described in adults.

papers.title: Germinal centers can persist for up to one year with declining somatic hypermutation and ongoing plasma cell output
papers.abstract: The total duration of primary germinal center (GC) responses, and how B cell evolution changes as these responses mature, remain poorly defined. Here, longitudinal sampling of rhesus macaques immunized with HIV Envelope protein revealed that a single slow-delivery prime sustained ongoing GCs for nearly a year without additional antigen. Somatic hypermutation (SHM) accumulated throughout these prolonged responses, but its rate declined substantially over time, independent of both priming strategy and boosting. Over the same period, subdominant non-base Env specificities became increasingly represented within the GC response. Delaying boosting until after primary GC contraction increased recruitment of recalled memory B cells into the GC response. Bone marrow plasma cells were generated throughout prolonged GC maturation, with the timing of their generation modulated by booster timing. Together, these findings reveal how GCs evolve across nearly a year and how this prolonged maturation shapes the memory and plasma cell compartments that underpin long-term humoral immunity.

papers.title: Clonotype specificity distinguishes epitope-tailored and permissive somatic hypermutation
papers.abstract: Identifying antibody features that reliably encode epitope specificity poses a major barrier towards modeling antigen-antibody interactions. Affinity maturation offers a unique opportunity to probe the molecular basis of antigen-antibody interactions by revealing how individual somatic hypermutations (SHM) refine antibody binding. Using SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific germinal center B-cell repertoires, we show that antibodies harboring multiple SHMs that are restricted to their respective clonotypes (clonotype-restricted SHMs) preferentially recognize cryptic epitopes. We structurally characterized three such antibodies: two recognized a cryptic epitope on the receptor-binding domain whereas a third bound an N-terminal domain epitope that is almost entirely occluded in prefusion spike. In contrast, SHMs shared across multiple clonotypes using the same V gene recur across antibodies targeting diverse antigens but generally fail to enhance affinity when introduced into diverse antibody backgrounds. Together, these findings define a spectrum of SHM behavior, distinguishing epitope-tailored mutations from broadly recurrent but largely permissive substitutions.

papers.title: Heterogeneity of HCMV-Specific CD8+ T Cells is Established Early in Infection, Clonally Encoded, and Stable Over Time
papers.abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (CMV) elicits lifelong memory T cell responses of striking size and phenotypic diversity, but how these diverse responses are established during acute infection and evolve over decades of chronic stimulation is poorly understood. We tracked CD8+ T cells specific for the viral antigens pp65 and IE1 by single-cell RNAseq, TCRseq, and CITEseq over a period of 16 months in a newly seroconverted donor, and in five latently infected donors over intervals ranging from 4.5 to 12.5 years. We found that individual T cell clones exhibited distinct, specificity-dependent transcriptional profiles, with pp65-specific cells skewed toward central memory phenotypes and IE1-specific cells enriched for effector and chronically activated states. Among pp65-specific T cells we identified a CMC1-expressing state not previously described in virus-specific T cells that shares transcriptional features with exhausted T cells in human tumors yet remains phenotypically stable and clonally intact for over a decade of viral latency. Distinct clonal phenotypes arose during acute infection and were remarkably stable during viral latency, and these phenotypes tracked with relative TCR avidity and TCR sequence. Our findings reveal that the phenotypic diversity of the human CMV-specific CD8+ T cell response is organized at the level of individual clones, with distinct functional identities established during acute infection and preserved with striking fidelity across decades of viral latency and chronic antigen exposure.

papers.title: A defined multi-kingdom microbial consortium naturalizes the immune system of laboratory mice
papers.abstract: Dirty mice experiments suggest that laboratory mice fail to model certain human immune responses due to their limited microbial exposure. The identity, nature, and number of microbes required to normalize the immune system are unknown. Through systematic screening, we uncovered unexpected cross-kingdom microbial interactions and identified four enteric microbes spanning viruses, fungi, and protists sufficient to reproduce key immunological features of pet store mice and adult humans. This consortium also altered cancer outcomes, shifting tumorigenesis toward the anatomical pattern of human familial adenomatous polyposis in ApcMin/+ mice and recapitulating the imperfect response of many patients to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy. Thus, surprisingly few microbes can profoundly reshape immune states and disease responses, providing a tractable approach to naturalize laboratory mouse immunity.

papers.title: Selective granzyme B replenishment dominates the molecular switch for sustained cytotoxicity in effector CD8+ T lymphocytes
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are highly efficient multiple killer cells, yet how they sustain killing after the initial discharge of canonical lytic granules remains incompletely understood. Late-phase cytotoxicity is often attributed to death receptor signaling or cytokine-mediated mechanisms, but whether CTLs also remodel their intrinsic cytotoxic machinery during prolonged engagement remains unclear. Here, we show that human CTLs maintain cytotoxic resilience through selective remodeling of their lytic program, marked by preferential preservation of granzyme B (GzmB). Following acute degranulation and reduction of mature perforin, CTLs selectively replenish GzmB through de novo protein synthesis, whereas perforin and several other granule-associated components show limited restoration. Replenished GzmB becomes redistributed into vesicular compartments with reduced overlap with mature perforin and is delivered to successive targets during sustained cytotoxic responses. Under conditions of limited detectable mature perforin, CTLs continue to deliver enzymatically active GzmB, induce altered calcium responses in target cells, and support productive but kinetically heterogeneous killing. This GzmB-preserved effector state is maintained and further accentuated during engagement with resistant melanoma cells. Together, our findings identify selective GzmB renewal as a central feature of sustained CTL cytotoxicity and reveal an adaptive remodeling of the cytotoxic machinery that may support CTL resilience during prolonged immune responses.

papers.title: Atypical T cell receptor signalling permits distinct gut gd T cell responses to healthy versus dysregulated tissues
papers.abstract: Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) are conserved across vertebrates and commonly enriched in {gamma}{delta} T cells. Several such {gamma}{delta} IELs depend upon homeostatic interactions of their T cell receptors (TCRs) with butyrophilin-like (BTNL) proteins expressed by healthy enterocytes and colonocytes. What limits such interactions from inducing full-blown T cell activation which would disrupt barrier integrity is unknown. Here, using primary IEL, we describe an atypical TCR signalling pathway (Signal 1) downstream of BTNL engagement, that fails to activate either global protein synthesis or cell proliferation. This attenuation could be overcome by provision of a co-stimulator (Signal 2) or inflammatory cytokines (Signal 3). It could also be relieved cell-intrinsically by blocking a lipid phosphatase. These findings can, at least in part, explain how extrinsic and intrinsic regulators permit IEL to be constitutively active in healthy tissues and additionally make full-blown responses to adaptive TCR ligands during tissue perturbation.

papers.title: mtDNA Activates AIM2-Mediated PANoptosis in Interstitial Macrophages to Promote Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Pneumonitis
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP) is a serious immune-related adverse event, yet its mechanisms remain unclear. Using a mouse model of anti-PD-1-induced CIP, we show that PD-1 blockade induces pulmonary inflammation and dysfunction, accompanied by accumulation of lung interstitial macrophages (IMs) and PANoptosis, preferentially in IMs rather than alveolar macrophages. Anti-PD-1 also causes mitochondrial stress and cytosolic mtDNA accumulation. AIM2 deficiency attenuates pulmonary inflammation, IM accumulation, and PANoptosis-associated signaling; NLRP3 or GSDMD deficiency similarly reduces inflammation and PANoptotic responses. In macrophages, TNF- plus IFN-{gamma} induces mitochondrial dysfunction and cytosolic mtDNA accumulation, and mtDNA amplifies cytokine-induced cell death and caspase-1/GSDMD activation, which is abolished by AIM2 deficiency. Thus, AIM2-mediated PANoptosis in lung IMs drives CIP, and mtDNA-associated innate immune signaling amplifies inflammatory macrophage death during CIP.

papers.title: Discovery of frameshift-associated TCRs following personalized neoantigen vaccination in a patient with osteosarcoma
papers.abstract: Personalized antigen-directed immunotherapies, including personalized cancer vaccines, are emerging as promising therapeutic modalities for a range of cancer types. Immune monitoring can be used to evaluate the efficacy of a vaccine in stimulating the immune response pre- and post-vaccination; however, such approaches typically stop short of identifying which T cell receptors (TCRs) are functionally driving therapeutic responses. Here, we present a case report of immune monitoring and subsequent TCR discovery experiments following administration of personalized cancer vaccines in a patient with locally recurrent osteosarcoma. Whole PBMCs were stimulated with vaccine peptides (>16 AA) in vitro for 11 days, after which IFN{gamma} ELISPOT identified total T cell responses for 12 of 15 tested peptides post-vaccination. In vitro expanded samples were submitted for 10x single-cell TCR sequencing, from which 26 TCRs were chosen for generation of TCR-T cells based on clonal expansion and culture specificity. Of the generated TCR-T cells, 25 produced functional TCRs, 4 of which were specific to vaccine peptides. However, downstream testing revealed each was MHC class-II restricted. To address this, we repeated the in vitro stimulations with co-cultures of isolated CD8+ T cells with autologous dendritic cells, and cultures of whole PBMCs with anti-MHC class-II blocking antibody. These cultures yielded 10 additional TCRs, 2 of which were responsive to a vaccine peptide containing a MAP2 frameshift mutation. These findings demonstrate an effective approach for leveraging post-vaccination expanded antigen-specific T cell populations for discovery of novel T cell receptors for downstream cellular therapies.

papers.title: Rationally Engineered Self-Assembling Protein Nanoparticles for Allergen-Specific Peanut Allergy Immunotherapy
papers.abstract: Peanut allergy is a prevalent immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated food allergy that can cause life-threatening anaphylaxis. Current treatment options provide limited efficacy and variable durability of protection. While allergen-displaying virus-like particles (VLPs) have shown promise, their development is often constrained by limited design flexibility and manufacturing complexity. Here, we develop self-assembling protein nanoparticles (SApNPs) displaying the major allergens Ara h 2 and Ara h 6 as a modular platform for peanut allergy immunotherapy. Using the 60-mer TIP60 scaffold, we engineer nanoparticles by expanding particle size through -helical insertion and replacing the human myosin-X segment with evolutionarily distant catfish homologs, followed by structure-guided and evolution-inspired optimization to enhance thermostability while minimizing human sequence content. Formulated with a Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) agonist, these allergen-displaying SApNPs confer robust protection against peanut-induced anaphylaxis in both prophylactic and therapeutic settings. Mechanistically, SApNPs exhibit prolonged lymph node retention, sustained presentation on follicular dendritic cells, and enhanced germinal center responses compared with soluble allergens, promoting allergen-specific IgG and functional T cell responses while limiting IgE escalation. Collectively, these findings establish allergen-displaying SApNPs as a rationally engineered, scalable, and modular platform for peanut allergy treatment with potential applicability to other allergic diseases.

papers.title: Xenoglycosylation of the HIV-1 Glycan Shield Promotes Cross-Clade Neutralization and Diverse Human Antibody Lineages
papers.abstract: Despite advances in HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein (Env)-based vaccine design, eliciting broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) remains a central challenge. Here, we identify core (1,3)-fucose as a key modulator of neutralizing antibody (NAb) induction and breadth. Uncleaved prefusion-optimized (UFO) trimers and self-assembling protein nanoparticles (SApNPs) produced in High Five (Hi5) insect cells incorporate core (1,3)-fucose into the Env glycan shield. Crystal structures of Hi5-produced BG505 UFO trimers in complex with bNAbs confirm native-like Env architecture and epitope presentation. In wild-type mice, these trimers and SApNPs elicit robust autologous and heterologous NAb responses. We then engineer Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells to co-express three insect- and plant-derived core (1,3)-fucosyltransferases. The resulting immunogens carry fucosylated mammalian glycans and elicit cross-clade NAb responses in mice, supporting an important role for core (1,3)-fucose in broadened neutralization. Env-specific IgE responses suggest engagement of associated immune pathways during vaccination. In ATX-Gx humanized mice, core (1,3)-fucosylated, glycan-trimmed Env elicits detectable cross-clade neutralization by week 11. Single-cell analysis identifies distinct human antibody lineages with cross-clade activity and noncanonical Env recognition. Repertoire and functional analyses uncover putatively related lineage members across two animals within the same group. Together, these findings support xenoglycosylation as a promising, germline-agnostic strategy for HIV-1 vaccine design.

papers.title: Cholesterol constrains pore formation by mammalian gasdermins
papers.abstract: Pyroptosis is a lytic form of cell death executed by gasdermin pores. Through a CRISPR screen to uncover macrophage genes required for gasdermin D (GSDMD) pore activity, we identify the endosome adaptor Rabgef1 as a positive regulator of pore formation. Rabgef1 deficiency preserves NT-GSDMD membrane binding but prevents NT-GSDMD oligomerization and lytic death. Mechanistic analyses revealed that Rabgef1 deficiency is associated with an overabundance of cholesterol in the plasma membrane. Cholesterol depletion or redistribution through multiple approaches restores GSDMD oligomerization and pyroptosis. The Rabgef1-mediated control of membrane cholesterol and pore formation was found to be a general regulator of the gasdermin family. In cancer cells, organoids, and tumors, cholesterol reduction sensitizes resistant cells to GSDME pyroptosis driven by synthetic mRNAs, chemogenetic induction, and chemotherapy treatment. These results establish membrane cholesterol content as an endogenous checkpoint for gasdermin-mediated pyroptotic cell death during the execution phase, with implications for metabolic disease and cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: A mosaic RBD-nanoparticle pan-sarbecovirus vaccine elicits nanobodies that target highly conserved epitopes
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, continually mutates, producing new variants of concern (VOCs). Substitutions in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein receptor-binding domain (RBD) have resulted in reduced efficacies of vaccines and therapeutic monoclonal antibodies. Indeed, since the emergence of Omicron and earlier VOCs, most previously approved anti-RBD therapeutic monoclonal antibodies are no longer authorized as therapeutics. To address VOC substitutions effects on therapeutic antibody efficacy, we sought to identify single-domain nanobodies (VHHs) targeting RBD regions (class 4, class 1/4, portions of class 3 and class 5 RBD epitopes) that are more conserved across VOCs, reasoning that the smaller size of camelid nanobodies compared with conventional two-domain antibody combining sites would facilitate access to occluded RBD epitopes. We used a Beacon optofluidic platform to isolate and characterize single memory B cells from a llama immunized with a mosaic RBD-nanoparticle immunogen that elicits broad antibody responses across sarbecoviruses. Using multiplex binding assays, we identified nanobodies that bind to spike RBDs from diverse sarbecovirus strains. Competition ELISAs and crystal structures of VHH-RBD complexes showed that isolated nanobodies recognize broadly conserved epitopes, including those on the RBD that are inaccessible to analogous conventional two-domain antibodies. Promising VHH-Fcs neutralized SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and zoonotic sarbecoviruses, demonstrating potential therapeutic utility for current and future outbreaks.

papers.title: Leishmania-infected human dendritic cells clear their intracellular parasites by a mechanism involving the cytolytic effector molecules granzyme B and granulysin
papers.abstract: Leishmania are intracellular parasites that cause various human diseases ranging from self-healing cutaneous to fatal visceral leishmaniasis. Host cells are phagocytes, primarily macrophages, where the parasites neutralize innate immune defenses, proliferate and finally rupture the cells. Despite that, Leishmania infection induces vigorous T cell responses, which require antigen processing and presentation, and stimulation by phagocytes, importantly dendritic cells. It was not clear how to align blockade of phagocyte functions with efficient immune stimulation. Here we show that, in contrast to macrophages, human dendritic cells survive the infection and destroy the parasites. This process involves granzyme B and granulysin, two cytolytic molecules essential for destruction of infected or otherwise aberrant cells by cytolytic T cells and natural killer cells. The report for the first time shows that these molecules not only act in target cell lysis by cytolytic effector cells but also in intracellular processing of infectious agents by dendritic cells.

papers.title: Dietary Exposure to Purified Gliadins and Avenins: Effects on Intestinal and Immune Responses in BALB/c Mice
papers.abstract: Dietary cereal prolamins differ in composition and gastrointestinal processing, but their shared and protein-source-specific effects on intestinal homeostasis remain incompletely defined. BALB/c mice were fed for five weeks with diets in which 70% of total protein was supplied by vital wheat gluten, purified gliadin, or purified avenin, alongside casein-fed controls. Intestinal morphology, antigen-specific plasma immunoglobulin G and A (IgG, IgA), mucosal gene expression, and small-intestinal proteomics were analysed. No overt histopathological injury or generalised inflammatory response was detected in any group. Gliadin and avenin both increased ileal villus length; avenin additionally elicited the broadest and most frequent prolamin-specific IgG response, associated with reduced intestinal interleukin-10 expression in responding animals. Proteomic profiling revealed a shared structural-metabolic signature alongside protein-specific changes in lipid handling, junctional regulation, and epithelial immune signalling. These findings indicate that wheat- and oat-derived prolamins differentially influence intestinal homeostasis and antigen recognition even at matched dietary doses, informing their evaluation as functional food ingredients.

papers.title: Structural Basis of γδ T-Cell Receptor Crosslinking and Activation by a Spontaneously Dimerized Fab
papers.abstract: The gamma delta T-cell receptor ({gamma}{delta} TCR) mediates {gamma}{delta} T-cell responses that are crucial for immune defense, tissue surveillance, and homeostasis. While recent studies suggest that {gamma}{delta} TCRs engage ligands multivalently, how multivalent engagement activates the {gamma}{delta} TCR remains elusive. Here, we present the structures of the V{gamma}9V{delta}2 (clone G115) TCR in both the inactive and the agonist-crosslinked active states. In the {gamma}{delta} TCR lipoprotein complex, cholesterol and phospholipids form a "barrier" that isolates CD3{zeta}{zeta} from the other subunits and likely prevents autoactivation. As an agonist, the Fab fragment of the UCHT1 antibody dimerizes upon binding the V{gamma}9V{delta}2 TCR, thereby crosslinking and activating the receptor. Cryo-EM analysis of Fab-crosslinked V{gamma}9V{delta}2 TCR identifies three Fab dimer interfaces, one between the two light chains and the other two between light and heavy chains. These Fab-Fab interfaces, together with the Fab-CD3{epsilon} interface, mediate the assembly of the V{gamma}9V{delta}2 TCR and UCHT1 Fab into 2:2 tetramers. Upon activation, the V{gamma}9V{delta}2 TCR becomes conformationally plastic and loses enriched lipids, including cholesterol and phosphatidylethanolamine. Our findings reveal a dimerization-driven activation mechanism, inform the design of rigid TCR-crosslinking agonists, and suggest multivalency-induced clustering as a general paradigm for {gamma}{delta} TCR activation.
